title: Utah Inspection Findings
question: In the Utah Risk Factor Study, which four inspection line items were more likely to be violations in summer, what were their rate ratios, and what limitations constrain interpretation of those findings?
final_result:
- In the Utah Risk Factor Study's summer vs. non-summer analysis (2016 data; summer defined as June, July, and August; alpha = 0.05), four line items were found to occur more frequently in summer months, and no line items were marked more frequently in non-summer months than in summer. [utah-risk-factor-study:p4:c0; utah-risk-factor-study:p4:c1]
- Line item 22 (Proper cold holding temperatures) had a summer rate ratio of 1.37 (95% LCL 1.23, 95% UCL 1.52; p < 0.005). [utah-risk-factor-study:p4:c1]
- Line item 33 (Proper cooling methods used; adequate equipment for temperature control) had the highest summer rate ratio at 1.50 (95% LCL 1.22, 95% UCL 1.86; p < 0.005). [utah-risk-factor-study:p4:c1]
- Line item 36 (Thermometers provided & accurate) had a summer rate ratio of 1.23 (95% LCL 1.04, 95% UCL 1.45; p < 0.025). [utah-risk-factor-study:p4:c1]
- Line item 28 (Toxic substances properly identified, stored, and used) had a summer rate ratio of 1.15 (95% LCL 1.02, 95% UCL 1.28; p < 0.025). [utah-risk-factor-study:p4:c1]
- The comparison was framed as a rate-ratio test of individual line item rates between summer and non-summer months using 95% confidence intervals, motivated by anecdotal (not established) evidence of seasonal variation. [utah-risk-factor-study:p3:c2]
- The rate ratios are conditional on a violation already occurring during an inspection ('Given that a violation occurs during an inspection'), so they describe the relative likelihood of a line item being marked, not overall violation rates. [utah-risk-factor-study:p4:c0]
- The study cautions that more data is needed before formulating a rationale for why toxic substance storage (line 28) would be in violation more often in summer, and that the line 36 finding may reflect inspectors examining thermometers more frequently in summer because of increased observations of temperature violations rather than a true increase in the problem. [utah-risk-factor-study:p6:c3]
- A stated limitation is participation: submission of data was voluntary, only seven of Utah's 13 local health departments volunteered data, and data were available for approximately 85% of Utah's population in 2016, with paper-record handling likely limiting broader participation. [utah-risk-factor-study:p4:c2; utah-risk-factor-study:p2:c1]
- Another limitation is that the analysis represents only a single year of inspection data that may not be representative of larger trends, and it looks only at the frequency of violations marked on the form; inadequate information makes it impossible to know the precise reasons a given line item was marked. [utah-risk-factor-study:p5:c2]
- Data-quality limitations also apply: all but two participating departments used inspection forms based on the 2009 Food Code that did not match the 2013 FDA form, so most line numbers had to be translated, and departments' rationales for categorizing establishments by risk were inconsistent, with no two departments categorizing establishments the same way. [utah-risk-factor-study:p5:c1; utah-risk-factor-study:p4:c2; utah-risk-factor-study:p7:c2]
- Interpreting the temperature-related findings, the study notes that kitchen temperatures over 90°F are reportedly not uncommon despite ventilation requirements (citing 6-304.11 of the 2013 FDA Food Code), and that cooling equipment efficiency declines past an ambient temperature limit, increasing the likelihood of temperature-abused food. [utah-risk-factor-study:p6:c2]
- These findings are historical Utah local inspection observations from 2016 (analysis conducted by UDOH with AFDO/FDA support) and are not a statement of current FDA model-code legal requirements. [utah-risk-factor-study:p2:c0; utah-risk-factor-study:p4:c1]

claims.text: In the Utah Risk Factor Study's summer vs. non-summer analysis (2016 data; summer defined as June, July, and August; alpha = 0.05), four line items were found to occur more frequently in summer months, and no line items were marked more frequently in non-summer months than in summer.
Line item 22 (Proper cold holding temperatures) had a summer rate ratio of 1.37 (95% LCL 1.23, 95% UCL 1.52; p < 0.005).
Line item 33 (Proper cooling methods used; adequate equipment for temperature control) had the highest summer rate ratio at 1.50 (95% LCL 1.22, 95% UCL 1.86; p < 0.005).
Line item 36 (Thermometers provided & accurate) had a summer rate ratio of 1.23 (95% LCL 1.04, 95% UCL 1.45; p < 0.025).
Line item 28 (Toxic substances properly identified, stored, and used) had a summer rate ratio of 1.15 (95% LCL 1.02, 95% UCL 1.28; p < 0.025).

The comparison was framed as a rate-ratio test of individual line item rates between summer and non-summer months using 95% confidence intervals, motivated by anecdotal (not established) evidence of seasonal variation.

The rate ratios are conditional on a violation already occurring during an inspection ('Given that a violation occurs during an inspection'), so they describe the relative likelihood of a line item being marked, not overall violation rates.

The study cautions that more data is needed before formulating a rationale for why toxic substance storage (line 28) would be in violation more often in summer, and that the line 36 finding may reflect inspectors examining thermometers more frequently in summer because of increased observations of temperature violations rather than a true increase in the problem.

A stated limitation is participation: submission of data was voluntary, only seven of Utah's 13 local health departments volunteered data, and data were available for approximately 85% of Utah's population in 2016, with paper-record handling likely limiting broader participation.

Another limitation is that the analysis represents only a single year of inspection data that may not be representative of larger trends, and it looks only at the frequency of violations marked on the form; inadequate information makes it impossible to know the precise reasons a given line item was marked.

Data-quality limitations also apply: all but two participating departments used inspection forms based on the 2009 Food Code that did not match the 2013 FDA form, so most line numbers had to be translated, and departments' rationales for categorizing establishments by risk were inconsistent, with no two departments categorizing establishments the same way.

Interpreting the temperature-related findings, the study notes that kitchen temperatures over 90°F are reportedly not uncommon despite ventilation requirements (citing 6-304.11 of the 2013 FDA Food Code), and that cooling equipment efficiency declines past an ambient temperature limit, increasing the likelihood of temperature-abused food.
These findings are historical Utah local inspection observations from 2016 (analysis conducted by UDOH with AFDO/FDA support) and are not a statement of current FDA model-code legal requirements.

Comparison of Violations Frequencies Between Summer and Non-Summer Months
Anecdotal evidence suggested that there may be seasonal variations in the frequency of line
item violations. To test this, rates of individual line items were compared between summer and non-
summer months. Summer months were defined as June, July, and August, with all other months
categorized as non-summer. Rate ratios between both time periods were compared using a 95%
confidence interval.

Correlation of Line Items
An analysis was done to determine if certain line items were more likely to occur given the
marking of a different line item. Correlations among pairs of line items 1 through 56 from the FDA form
were compared using a Phi correlation coefficient. Only line item pairs with -0.80 => r >= +0.80 were
reported as being meaningful. This cutoff was chosen to focus on the strongest line item pair
correlations.

Limitations:
Of the 13 local health departments, seven volunteered data for use in this study. More than half
of the local health departments currently use a method for storing inspection data digitally; the rest
keep inspection hard copies. One health department sent in scanned copies of inspection data, which
needed to be inputted manually. The time and labor involved with sending, collating, and scanning in
copies of paper inspections likely limited broader participation by the local health departments.

This analysis is dependent on the ability to categorize establishments based on inherent risk due
to populations served, types of food served, and type of food preparation techniques used. Though the
rationales for categorizing establishments were inconsistent from one health department to another,
each did use a classification system using some form of risk. The types of classifications being used by

In Conclusion:
The primary conclusion from this study is that more training needs to be done with inspectors
on risk based inspection methods. Such training should include some of the training given when doing
standardizations, specifically training on the use of the FDA form. Additional information may be
needed to be given to inspectors on when certain line items should be marked.

These results also highlight the need for greater awareness among operators of the importance
of keeping their kitchens cool and of adequate ventilation. Also, keeping hand sinks clear of clutter and
knowing how to maintain their dishwashers should be emphasized. These conclusions will be discussed
with the local health department along with potential future training opportunities.

results.text:
Foodborne illnesses continue to be a public health concern in Utah. Utah’s local health
departments are responsible to inspect food service businesses in Utah and to respond to foodborne
illness complaints or outbreaks. The Utah Department of Health (UDOH) provides training and support
to the local health departments. In addition, UDOH oversees and administers rules and policies that
provide regulatory standards of operation for food safety and authority for local health departments to
enforce those standards. The UDOH conducted an analysis of data from retail food inspections
conducted in 2016 by local inspectors. This analysis was done through a cooperative agreement with
the Association of Food and Drug Officials (AFDO) administering a grant from the U.S. Food and Drug
Administration (FDA).

Purpose:
The purpose of this analysis is to evaluate trends, patterns, and correlations of food code
violations with the intent of finding ways of improving the efficacy and efficiency of food establishment
inspections by local departments, and to identify priorities for focused training and policy development
by UDOH.

claims.text: In the Utah Risk Factor Study's summer vs. non-summer analysis (2016 data; summer defined as June, July, and August; alpha = 0.05), four line items were found to occur more frequently in summer months, and no line items were marked more frequently in non-summer months than in summer.
Line item 22 (Proper cold holding temperatures) had a summer rate ratio of 1.37 (95% LCL 1.23, 95% UCL 1.52; p < 0.005).
Line item 33 (Proper cooling methods used; adequate equipment for temperature control) had the highest summer rate ratio at 1.50 (95% LCL 1.22, 95% UCL 1.86; p < 0.005).
Line item 36 (Thermometers provided & accurate) had a summer rate ratio of 1.23 (95% LCL 1.04, 95% UCL 1.45; p < 0.025).
Line item 28 (Toxic substances properly identified, stored, and used) had a summer rate ratio of 1.15 (95% LCL 1.02, 95% UCL 1.28; p < 0.025).

The comparison was framed as a rate-ratio test of individual line item rates between summer and non-summer months using 95% confidence intervals, motivated by anecdotal (not established) evidence of seasonal variation.

The rate ratios are conditional on a violation already occurring during an inspection ('Given that a violation occurs during an inspection'), so they describe the relative likelihood of a line item being marked, not overall violation rates.

The study cautions that more data is needed before formulating a rationale for why toxic substance storage (line 28) would be in violation more often in summer, and that the line 36 finding may reflect inspectors examining thermometers more frequently in summer because of increased observations of temperature violations rather than a true increase in the problem.

A stated limitation is participation: submission of data was voluntary, only seven of Utah's 13 local health departments volunteered data, and data were available for approximately 85% of Utah's population in 2016, with paper-record handling likely limiting broader participation.

Another limitation is that the analysis represents only a single year of inspection data that may not be representative of larger trends, and it looks only at the frequency of violations marked on the form; inadequate information makes it impossible to know the precise reasons a given line item was marked.

Data-quality limitations also apply: all but two participating departments used inspection forms based on the 2009 Food Code that did not match the 2013 FDA form, so most line numbers had to be translated, and departments' rationales for categorizing establishments by risk were inconsistent, with no two departments categorizing establishments the same way.

Interpreting the temperature-related findings, the study notes that kitchen temperatures over 90°F are reportedly not uncommon despite ventilation requirements (citing 6-304.11 of the 2013 FDA Food Code), and that cooling equipment efficiency declines past an ambient temperature limit, increasing the likelihood of temperature-abused food.
These findings are historical Utah local inspection observations from 2016 (analysis conducted by UDOH with AFDO/FDA support) and are not a statement of current FDA model-code legal requirements.
